title: Attempt Seven

pages.text:
*Percy's Error Log, Entry 24, later still. Attempt: 7. Result: see below.*

The gymnasium was silent, except for the wet drip of foam from the ceiling and the soft squeak of sneakers on the polished floor. Parents and students stood in a wide, wary circle. The machine lay in a twisted heap of plastic and wire, a monument to our collective exhaustion. I looked at the crowd, then at Ms. Adeyemi, who was wiping a streak of blue foam from her cardigan with a grimace.

"Ms. Adeyemi," I said. My voice was quiet, but it carried. "We may try once more."

She looked at the exhausted faces of the children, their hair matted, their clothes ruined. She looked at the parents, who were staring intently at the wreckage. She looked at me. I did not move. I did not blink. My chest light was steady, a small point of blue in the dimness.

"The decision," she said, "does not belong to me. It belongs to the people who built it."

Bea Alvarado stepped forward. She was trembling, a pencil still stuck in her messy bun, her goggles askew. She looked at the wreckage, then at me. A slow smile spread across her face, wiping away the fear.

"One more," she said.
pages.image: A tall silver-white robot with round blue eyes stands in a dim gymnasium, looking at a teacher in a head-wrap who is wiping blue foam from her cardigan. A short girl in a yellow raincoat with pencils in her hair smiles determinedly nearby.

pages.text:
We reset the machine in twelve minutes. It was not a fast process, but it was a kind one. Parents knelt on the floor, using sponges to clean the sticky residue from the gears. Someone brought a bucket of warm water. The brass band, which had been silent, began to play a slow, dignified march. It was the wrong tempo for the work, but it helped. We moved the dominoes. We aligned the levers. We checked the tension on the springs.

Tobias Pym stood by the base of the machine, his bow tie askew. He was wiping his glasses with a handkerchief that was more foam than fabric. He looked at the crowd, which had not left. Four hundred people stood in the stands, watching the foam dry in their hair.

"I do not know if this will work," Tobias said. His voice was thin, but steady. He looked at me, and I saw something in his eyes that I had not seen before. It was not fear. It was readiness. "I am going to be wrong in front of four hundred people. This is fine."
pages.image: A thin boy in a bow tie wipes his glasses with a suds-covered handkerchief while standing next to a complex machine made of plastic and wire. In the background, a brass band plays while parents kneel on the gym floor cleaning gears.

pages.text:
I kept my hands behind my back, resisting the urge to guide the marble or steady the lever, while I stood in the center of the machine like a silver figure in a sea of plastic and hope. Ms. Adeyemi nodded, and I nodded back.

The marble rolled out of its track, a small white sphere moving with the heavy, deliberate slowness of a thing that knows it is being watched. It hit the first domino, which fell and tipped the bucket, launching the car across the gym floor.

The lever moved.

It was a single, sharp click, but it sounded like a thunderclap. A link dropped, then another, and a marble fell into a cup with a hollow thud. The fan spun up, blowing dust into the air, while the windmill turned, slow and steady.

The crowd began to count.

"Thirty-one," someone whispered.
"Thirty-two," another voice added.
"Thirty-three!"

The parrot, who had been quiet, opened its beak and shouted, "Not yet!" at every single number. It was the funniest thing I had ever heard.
pages.image: A white marble rolls down a plastic track on a large machine, knocking over a domino. A tall silver robot stands with hands behind his back. In the stands, a crowd watches intently, and a parrot on a perch shouts with its beak open.

pages.text:
Link thirty-eight was a wheel, no bigger than a dinner plate, and it had jammed. The whole mechanism shuddered to a halt, leaving the gymnasium in a sudden, heavy silence. Four hundred people stopped moving, creating a vacuum that seemed to suck the air straight out of the room.

Then, a small paw reached in from the side.

It was Gerald. He had escaped his cage again and was running along the frame, his tiny legs blurring like a fast-forwarded video game clip. He stopped at the jammed wheel, looked up at me, and tapped the metal with a precise, gentle paw.

The wheel turned.

Forty. Forty-one.

The foam tube coughed, releasing one small puff of white mist. Then, a paper flag rose from the top of the machine. It was crooked and slightly torn, which made it perfect.
pages.image: A round fawn-and-white hamster stands on a plastic frame, tapping a small wheel with its paw. A tall silver robot watches with wide blue eyes. A paper flag rises from the top of the machine, slightly crooked.

pages.text:
For a second, nobody breathed. The flag hung there, trembling in the still air. Then the gym erupted. It was a roar, a physical wave of sound that hit me in the chest and pushed me back half a step. Hundreds of people were hugging strangers. The brass band was playing the wrong song, a fast, jagged melody that matched the joy of the moment.

I stood in the middle of it, my chest light shining so brightly that the ceiling above me turned gold. I did not feel proud. I felt full. I felt seen.

Bea was running across the stage. She was not looking at the crowd. She was looking at her notebook, the Failure Journal. She opened it to a fresh page. Her hand shook as she wrote, in large, capital letters:

WORKED.

She looked up at me and laughed. It was the best sound I have ever processed.
pages.image: A tall silver robot stands in the center of a gymnasium, his chest light glowing bright gold. A short girl in a yellow raincoat sits on the floor, writing in a small notebook with a pencil, smiling up at him. The background is a blur of cheering people.
